title: Bias and Unfairness in Machine Learning Models: A Systematic Review on Datasets, Tools, Fairness Metrics, and Identification and Mitigation Methods
explain_beginner: This review looked at research on fairness in machine learning, the systems that make decisions from data. The authors searched several databases and selected 45 studies from 2017 to 2022. They found that most work tries to find or reduce bias, using datasets, tools, and fairness measures. Common measures include Equalized Odds, Opportunity Equality, and Demographic Parity. The studies cover areas like criminal justice, finance, education, pricing, and health. A key point is that different fairness measures can disagree about the same case. So an audit should say which measure it used and why. More varied research is still needed.
explain_business: This review shows that fairness in machine learning is not a single, settled standard. Organizations using automated decisions should expect different fairness measures to give conflicting answers for the same case. That means an audit or governance process must name the fairness measure used and explain why it fits the context. The paper also finds limited research on multiclass and multimetric settings, so many methods remain binary focused. For executives, this supports cautious deployment, clear documentation, and asking vendors or teams which fairness definition they applied. It also informs investment in broader testing across model types and use cases before relying on fairness claims.
explain_practitioner: The authors conducted a PRISMA systematic review, registered on OSF, searching Scopus, IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, and Google Scholar from 2021 to early 2022. They identified 128 articles from 2017 to 2022 and selected 45 after refining the search and applying screening rules. The review maps datasets, tools, metrics, and methods for finding and reducing bias. It reports bias from data, algorithms, and user interaction linked to preprocessing, during processing, and postprocessing fixes. Equalized Odds, Opportunity Equality, and Demographic Parity are primary metrics. Aequitas is most cited, though many tools lack empirical use. Result: fairness metrics can disagree for one use case, and multiclass or multimetric studies are scarce.
